headings.title: Introduction and Purpose of Intravenous Infusion
headings.content: Intravenous (IV) infusion is a core clinical competency for nursing students practicing in Nigeria and globally. It involves the direct administration of fluids, electrolytes, medications, blood products, or total parenteral nutrition into the venous system. The primary purpose of IV therapy is to restore and maintain fluid and electrolyte balance, correct acid-base disturbances, administer medications rapidly, and provide nutritional support when the gastrointestinal tract is compromised. Unlike oral routes, IV therapy provides immediate bioavailability, making it essential in emergency situations such as severe dehydration from gastroenteritis, shock, or trauma. Nurses must understand the physiological implications of fluid administration, as improper management can lead to rapid circulatory overload or failure to correct deficits. Patient assessment is vital before initiating any infusion; the nurse must review the medical prescription, check the patient's identity, evaluate baseline vital signs, and assess the status of the peripheral veins. Furthermore, strict adherence to aseptic technique is non-negotiable to prevent hospital-acquired bloodstream infections. In the Nigerian healthcare context, where resource limitations may sometimes challenge equipment availability, improvising safely while maintaining sterility remains a critical skill. By mastering the fundamentals of IV therapy, student nurses lay the groundwork for safe, effective clinical practice, ensuring optimal patient outcomes across diverse healthcare settings.

headings.title: Anatomy and Selection of Peripheral Veins
headings.content: Selecting an appropriate peripheral vein is critical for successful intravenous cannulation and the prevention of complications. Common sites for peripheral IV access include the dorsal venous network of the hand, the cephalic and basilic veins of the forearm, and sometimes the veins in the antecubital fossa, though the latter should be avoided if possible because flexion of the arm can occlude the catheter. When assessing a patient's veins, the nurse should start from the distal areas of the upper extremities and move proximally, preserving upper sites for potential future cannulation. Ideal veins feel soft, straight, bouncy, and refill promptly after release. Nurses should avoid veins in an extremity that is paralyzed, affected by a stroke, compromised by lymphedema (such as the arm on the side of a mastectomy), or containing a dialysis shunt, as these areas are high-risk for severe complications. Palpation and visual inspection are key assessment techniques; applying a tourniquet temporarily engorges the vessel, making it easier to visualize and palpate. Veins that are sclerosed, tortuous, inflamed, or located near areas of recent trauma or infection must be avoided. By choosing the most suitable vein and matching it with an appropriately sized cannula, the nurse minimizes patient discomfort, reduces the risk of infiltration or phlebitis, and ensures the prescribed therapy can be delivered effectively throughout its intended duration.

headings.title: Types of Intravenous Solutions and Fluids
headings.content: Intravenous solutions are categorized based on their osmolality relative to blood plasma, which dictates how fluid shifts between the intravascular compartment and the cells. Isotonic solutions, such as 0.9% Normal Saline and Lactated Ringer's solution, have an osmolality similar to extracellular fluid and are primarily used for extracellular volume expansion, such as in hemorrhage or severe dehydration, because they do not cause fluid to shift into or out of cells. Hypotonic solutions, such as 0.45% Normal Saline, have a lower osmolality than serum and cause water to move out of the intravascular space and into the intracellular and interstitial compartments, making them useful for treating cellular dehydration like diabetic ketoacidosis. Hypertonic solutions, such as 5% Dextrose in 0.9% Normal Saline or 10% Dextrose in Water, possess a higher osmolality than serum, drawing water out of the cells and into the vascular space to reduce cerebral edema or correct severe hyponatremia. Nurses must carefully verify the specific fluid ordered, monitor the patient's hydration status, and watch for signs of fluid overload or electrolyte imbalances. Understanding these fluid dynamics is vital for safe nursing practice, as administering the wrong tonicity can lead to rapid cellular damage, hemolysis, or pulmonary edema, particularly in vulnerable populations such as pediatric and geriatric patients.

headings.title: Equipment Needed for IV Cannulation and Infusion
headings.content: Successful intravenous therapy requires gathering and organizing the correct equipment before approaching the patient, ensuring efficiency and minimizing infection risks. Essential items include the prescribed IV fluid bag, an administration set (either macro-drip or micro-drip tubing depending on the flow rate and patient age), an IV cannula of appropriate gauge (such as 18G for rapid fluid resuscitation, 20G or 22G for standard infusions, and 24G for pediatrics), a tourniquet, antiseptic skin cleansing swabs (such as 70% alcohol or chlorhexidine), sterile transparent dressings or adhesive tape, a sterile extension set or injection cap if needed, non-sterile gloves, and a sharps container. The nurse must check the expiry dates and integrity of all packaging, especially the IV fluid bag to ensure there is no discoloration, turbidity, or leakage. Having an infusion stand ( drip stand) ready and accessible is also crucial. Proper organization of the bedside workstation facilitates a smooth procedure and prevents breaks in aseptic technique. In clinical settings across Nigeria, ensuring all these materials are assembled before breaking skin integrity reduces patient anxiety and prevents the need to leave the patient unattended mid-procedure. Familiarity with every piece of equipment empowers student nurses to act decisively and maintain a sterile, safe environment.

headings.title: Step-by-Step Procedure for IV Cannulation
headings.content: Performing IV cannulation requires precision, confidence, and strict adherence to infection control principles. The nurse begins by explaining the procedure to the patient and obtaining informed consent. After performing hand hygiene and donning non-sterile gloves, the nurse applies a tourniquet 10 to 15 cm above the chosen insertion site and selects a suitable vein. The skin is cleansed thoroughly using an antiseptic swab in a circular motion from the center outward and allowed to air dry completely to ensure maximum antimicrobial efficacy. The nurse stabilizes the vein by pulling the skin taut distally, holding the cannula with the bevel facing upward at an angle of 15 to 30 degrees. The skin and vein wall are punctured in one smooth motion; upon seeing a flashback of blood in the chamber, the nurse advances the cannula slightly further and then slides the catheter off the needle into the vein while withdrawing the stylet. The safety mechanism of the needle is activated immediately, and the tourniquet is released. The administration set tubing is connected quickly and securely to the hub, and the flow is adjusted. Finally, a sterile transparent dressing is applied over the site to secure the catheter and allow for continuous visual inspection, and the tubing is taped securely to the skin. Documenting the date, time, cannula size, and site in the patient's record concludes the procedure.

headings.title: Calculating and Regulating Infusion Flow Rates
headings.content: Calculating and regulating infusion flow rates is a vital nursing responsibility that prevents both fluid volume deficit and fluid overload. The nurse must calculate the correct flow rate based on the total volume to be infused, the total time prescribed, and the drop factor of the administration set (which is usually found on the packaging, such as 15 drops/mL for standard sets or 60 drops/mL for micro-drip sets). The standard formula used is: (Total Volume in mL × Drop Factor) / Total Time in Minutes = Drops per Minute (gtts/min). Alternatively, when calculating millilitres per hour (mL/hr), the total volume is divided by the total hours. Once the mathematical calculation is complete, the nurse adjusts the roller clamp on the administration set while counting the drops dripping into the drip chamber over a full minute using a watch with a second hand. Electronic infusion pumps, when available, offer precise automated control and feature safety alarms for occlusion or air in the line, though manual regulation via gravity remains common in many resource-limited Nigerian clinical environments. Nurses must reassess flow rates frequently, as patient movement, positional changes of the limb, or changes in vein patency can alter the rate, risking complications like pulmonary edema if fluids infuse too rapidly.

headings.title: Ongoing Nursing Monitoring and Maintenance
headings.content: Ongoing nursing monitoring and maintenance are essential to ensure the continuous patency of the IV line and the safety of the patient throughout therapy. The nurse should perform regular assessments of the insertion site at least every shift or according to hospital protocol, checking for signs of redness, swelling, tenderness, warmth, or fluid leakage. The infusion tubing, fluid bags, and dressing changes must adhere to strict institutional schedules; typically, continuous tubing is replaced every 72 to 96 hours, while intermittent sets are changed more frequently. The nurse must also monitor the patient's systemic response, assessing vital signs regularly, auscultating breath sounds for early signs of fluid overload (such as crackles), and checking intake and output charts to ensure balanced fluid management. Flushing the intermittent injection cap or saline lock with normal saline before and after medication administration maintains patency and prevents blood clotting within the catheter. If any resistance is felt when flushing, the nurse must never force it, as this can dislodge a blood clot into the circulation; instead, troubleshooting steps should be taken. Maintaining a clean, dry, and intact dressing protects the site from microbial invasion. Through vigilant monitoring, nurses catch minor issues before they escalate into major systemic complications.

headings.title: Complications of Intravenous Therapy and Management
headings.content: Intravenous therapy carries several potential local and systemic complications that require prompt recognition and expert nursing management. Local complications include infiltration (where non-vesicant fluid leaks into surrounding tissue), extravasation (where a vesicant medication leaks, causing tissue necrosis), phlebitis (inflammation of the vein wall characterized by pain, erythema, and a palpable cord), thrombophlebitis, and local hematoma formation at the puncture site. If any of these local signs occur, the nurse must immediately stop the infusion, disconnect the tubing, carefully remove the cannula, elevate the extremity, and apply warm or cold compresses depending on the type of fluid or medication involved, reporting the incident to the physician. Systemic complications are more dangerous and include circulatory fluid overload (manifested by hypertension, dyspnea, engorged neck veins, and crackles), air embolism (caused by air entering the vascular system through unprimed tubing), sepsis, and allergic or anaphylactic reactions to infused medications or blood products. Management of systemic issues requires immediate cessation of the infusion, notifying the physician, administering emergency medications or oxygen as ordered, and supporting vital life functions. Vigilant nursing care is the primary defense against these adverse events.

headings.title: Discontinuation of Intravenous Infusion
headings.content: Discontinuation of an intravenous infusion is performed when therapy is completed, the prescription is changed, or complications such as infiltration or phlebitis develop. The nurse begins by explaining the procedure to the patient, verifying the order, and performing hand hygiene before donning non-sterile gloves. The roller clamp on the administration set is closed to stop the flow of fluid. The nurse gently removes the adhesive dressing and stabilization tape surrounding the insertion site, taking care not to pull on the catheter or traumatize the skin. A sterile dry gauze pad or cotton ball is placed gently over the insertion site without applying pressure while the catheter is withdrawn smoothly and parallel to the skin to avoid trauma to the vessel wall. Once the catheter is completely removed, immediate pressure is applied to the site using the gauze for at least one to two minutes until hemostasis is achieved, especially if the patient has a bleeding disorder or is on anticoagulants. The nurse inspects the removed catheter to ensure it is intact and that the tip has not broken off inside the vein. Finally, a clean adhesive bandage or plaster is applied over the site, the used equipment is disposed of properly according to waste management protocols (with needles going into a sharps box), and the discontinuation is accurately documented in the patient's medical record.
